title: Crystalline-silicon PV: changing markets and production capabilities
summary: A linked set of episodes distinguishes early terrestrial-market formation, later module process improvements, and Chinese producer entry from domestic deployment. The evidence tests learning-only and cheap-labour-only explanations.

stages.invention: Prehistory; no single invention date established here.
stages.feasibility: Repeatable crystalline-silicon cell/module production existed before the sampled expansion; subsequent yield and material improvements measured in reconstructed models.
stages.deployment: US space and off-grid terrestrial tasks in the 1970s; later policy-supported grid markets in Japan/Europe.
stages.diffusion: Dated Chinese production/export shares and qualitative supplier/worker knowledge circulation; no household adopter census.
stages.scaling: Factory size, efficiency, material use/prices and process yield changed during 1980–2012.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Early terrestrial niches and very small Chinese domestic-demand share despite major export manufacturing.
stages.displacement/reversal: No general displacement of fossil generation or quantification of net welfare established.

counterevidence: Decomposition allocations differ strongly by model; low wages, energy cost, finance, foreign incentives and technology transfer covary.

episode.technology_configuration: Crystalline-silicon modules; subepisodes: worldwide PV prices with partly US market-formation examples (1970s), worldwide production-cost reconstructions (1980–2012), Chinese downstream entry (2003–2009).
episode.task: Provide electrical energy in remote/space tasks and later grid-connected installations; produce saleable modules meeting market quality.
episode.population: Module manufacturers/industry averages in cost studies; selected Chinese firms and equipment suppliers in interview/patent study; installations are only indirectly observed.
episode.interval: 1970–2012, with nonidentical subepisode windows explicitly separated.
contemporary_alternatives: Spacecraft primary batteries for finite missions
Remote diesel or extending electricity connections where feasible
Other PV chemistries; not cost-equivalent in every sampled period
episode.adoption_measure: Worldwide module price/cost reconstructions with partly US contextual market examples; 2008 Chinese world-production/export shares; separate 2009 global-demand share. No common adopter denominator across subepisodes.
episode.observation_limits: Module manufacture is not installed-system service; nominal output is not lifetime energy; model variables mix sources and interviews select producers.

actors.chooser: Space/remote-system purchasers, later system owners under national support regimes, and firms choosing production investment.
actors.payer: Government procurement/public research; private firm capital; tariff/tax-supported customers in later grid markets; individual financing shares not identified.
actors.operator_maintainer: Manufacturing engineers, technicians and production workers; system installers and owners. Vendor training is documented.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Ratepayers/taxpayers, production communities and workers; their net burdens/benefits were not measured in these studies.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Producer entry is a firm choice; downstream buyers face task and connection constraints. Foreign recruitment/no-poach arrangements are reported, but worker consent, legal enforceability and household ability to decline support costs are not established.

labour.tasks: Vendor training, line operation/adaptation, quality control, manual/automated module assembly, recruitment of experienced managers.
labour.entry_barriers: Skilled process knowledge and capital; accessible downstream turnkey equipment reduced some firm-entry barriers, while upstream secrecy and limited suppliers impeded entry.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Firms controlled equipment and hiring. Interviews report poaching disputes and agreements not to recruit rivals’ skilled staff; wage/bargaining effects unmeasured.
labour.transition: Some executive migration histories documented; no longitudinal worker transition or retraining cohort.
labour.distribution: Distinct opportunities for internationally trained managers versus assembly tasks; no reliable wages, gender, working-condition or displaced-worker distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Reduced labour cost per module cannot establish fewer total jobs, better livelihoods or who retained gains.

title: Nuclear construction: coordinated programmes, cost variation and finance boundaries
period: Construction cohorts 1954–2008; French programme 1970–2000; US accounting 1976–1987 and cancellation context 2017
summary: National completed-project cost histories and component accounts challenge both automatic learning and inevitable escalation. Rapid coordinated construction can coexist with rising unit costs; finance and cancellations remain outside overnight-cost trends.

stages.invention: Nuclear fission/reactor invention precedes this construction comparison; no invention claim made.
stages.feasibility: Commercial reactor configurations were imported, licensed, standardized and revised; feasibility did not settle project cost.
stages.deployment: France built a large PWR fleet under concentrated procurement; South Korea adopted commercial imports and domestic derivatives.
stages.diffusion: Installed fleets and construction cohorts, not individual electricity-user choices.
stages.scaling: Bulk orders, domestic manufacturing/engineering and multi-unit projects; cost effects differ by cohort and site.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Completed-reactor datasets omit cancelled proposals and selected experimental designs.
stages.displacement/reversal: VC Summer expansion abandoned in 2017 in the inspected US account; no systematic cancellation rate estimated.

counterevidence: Cross-country trajectories are not matched experiments; interest excluded, cancellations missing, and later French data revise earlier estimates.

episode.technology_configuration: Commercial power-reactor cohorts; France PWR programme; Korea imported and domestic designs; US Westinghouse four-loop cost accounts, with 2017 cancellation as a separate outcome.
episode.task: Construct and operate grid-connected bulk electricity supply under national security, economic and regulatory objectives.
episode.population: 349 reactors in seven-country compilation (focus US/France/Korea), completed-project selection; EEDB representative US plant accounts are a different population.
episode.interval: Country construction-start cohorts through 2008 in the historical compilation; US accounting 1976–1987; historical cancellation observed in 2017.
contemporary_alternatives: Coal/oil/gas generation under period-specific fuel prices
Different reactor designs, imported or domestic
episode.adoption_measure: Completed reactor capacity/cohorts and construction time; overnight currency per kW in 2010 domestic prices. No uniform whole-project adoption hazard.
episode.observation_limits: Missing proposed/cancelled projects, financing, some experimental routes and major countries; different technologies, periods, deflators and record quality.

actors.chooser: Government/utility planners, regulators, reactor vendors and financing authorities; households generally did not choose the generation fleet.
actors.payer: Utility capital, lenders and state-backed programmes, ultimately allocated through rates/taxes or losses; precise incidence not quantified.
actors.operator_maintainer: Engineering organizations, construction contractors, plant operators and fuel-cycle workers.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Electricity customers, site communities, construction workers, waste/fuel-cycle communities and taxpayers.
actors.ability_to_refuse: France’s history describes concentrated technocratic decisions and weak public influence; this is not consent. Korean community/worker refusal channels and US project-level bargaining are unestablished in inspected cost records.

labour.tasks: Engineering design, scheduling, purchasing, on-site supervision, construction and quality assurance; operation continues after construction.
labour.entry_barriers: Large capital commitments, engineering capability, qualified vendors and safety requirements; individual credential thresholds not reconstructed.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Utility/vendor/state control of project choices; cost accounts reveal expenditure rather than worker bargaining or who absorbs overruns.
labour.transition: No worker/cohort tracking across construction pauses or cancelled plants; costs cannot establish retraining outcomes.
labour.distribution: Higher indirect spending is observed in a model; no supported wage, employment-security or regional-income distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Cost and completion histories cannot settle occupational gains, welfare, accident risk or benefits from avoided fossil pollution.

title: Planar silicon and merchant DRAM: reproducibility, procurement and bounded learning
summary: Two explicitly distinct episodes connect protected-junction manufacturing and Apollo procurement to later tests of generation-specific DRAM learning. The evidence rejects patent-equals-diffusion and simple national-learning-superiority stories.

stages.invention: Hoerni’s coating-retention method disclosed in 1959 patent application; no claim to exclusive invention of the transistor or IC.
stages.feasibility: Working planar transistor recorded in March 1959; repeatability and continuing failure mechanisms distinguished from a patent.
stages.deployment: Commercial planar transistor in April 1960; Apollo NOR-gate purchases in the early 1960s.
stages.diffusion: Commercial licensing described qualitatively; later 32-firm merchant-DRAM shipment panel.
stages.scaling: Standardized procurement and inferred within-generation production learning; direct yield panel absent.
stages.non-adoption/niche: High-value spacecraft niche precedes broad consumer affordability; core/transistor alternatives were considered.
stages.displacement/reversal: DRAM generation transitions include entry and exit; they do not establish whole-firm disappearance.

counterevidence: Later DRAM evidence does not identify what Apollo caused; patent, museum and official history share inherited records and lack full factory data.

episode.technology_configuration: Episode A: silicon planar transistor process and Apollo NOR logic, 1957–1969. Episode B: merchant DRAM generations 4K through 16M, 1974–1992. No transitive causal proof is asserted between episodes.
episode.task: Manufacture reliable compact switching/logic devices and, separately, inexpensive merchant memory.
episode.population: Fairchild/process-history and Apollo engineering records; separate Dataquest panel of 32 merchant firms, excluding internal-only producers.
contemporary_alternatives: Different gates and redundant/repairable computer designs
Internal rather than merchant memory production
episode.adoption_measure: Documented prototype/product introduction and NASA purchase episode; later quarterly DRAM shipments/prices, not direct costs or plant yields.
episode.observation_limits: Patent is not proof of uptake; procurement share is narrow in time; structural model infers cost from price/output and market assumptions.

actors.chooser: Device firms, NASA/MIT system designers and merchant-memory producers; buyers chose different performance/cost trade-offs.
actors.payer: Corporate investment and publicly financed Apollo procurement; later merchant sales and investment, exact R&D/procurement shares unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Process engineers, fabrication and test workers, equipment/quality specialists and system designers.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Taxpayers and manufacturing workers/communities; hazardous-material exposure and labour allocation are not quantified here.
actors.ability_to_refuse: System designers evaluated alternatives; firms could enter/exit merchant product lines. Workers’ employment alternatives, compelled transfers and local community voice unknown.

labour.tasks: Protective coating/masking/diffusion, contact and packaging work, qualification tests, defect diagnosis, production-process monitoring.
labour.entry_barriers: Precision/cleanliness, equipment, process knowledge and capital. Cross-generation spillover estimates do not measure every entry barrier.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Patent assigned to Fairchild and rights licensed according to museum account; firms own production assets. Worker bargaining evidence absent.
labour.transition: Firm-level product entry/exit observed; no individual transitions from wiring/assembly to fabrication quantified.
labour.distribution: Model tests country-level learning rates; it does not measure wage inequality, gendered assembly work or ownership returns.
labour.evidence_limit: No claim that semiconductor learning automatically creates accessible work or that 20% inferred cost learning means a 20% labour-productivity gain.

title: Lithium-ion cells: feasible chemistry, qualification and manufacturing improvement
summary: A first-person development account and later fixed-format cell model distinguish rechargeable chemistry from saleable qualification and from the sources of cost improvement. No universal battery-replacement or safety claim follows.

stages.invention: Several electrode discoveries and configurations; Yoshino’s carbon/lithiated-cathode patent in 1985 is one development, not a sole-inventor story.
stages.feasibility: Laboratory rechargeable operation faced heat, volume and abuse-performance constraints; paired material selection and testing mattered.
stages.deployment: Commercial manufacture/sales in Japan in 1991 reported by Yoshino.
stages.diffusion: Portable-electronics use is described qualitatively; no independently audited adopter count.
stages.scaling: Cost and component changes for representative high-energy 18650 cells between two multi-year windows.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Rejected PA and metallic-lithium configurations in the described pathway; application-specific needs persist.
stages.displacement/reversal: No assertion that Li-ion displaced every rechargeable chemistry; ENE-C05 records continued lead-acid use.

counterevidence: Inventor selection and incomplete process records; cell format, power, safety and cycle-life trade-offs limit aggregation.

episode.technology_configuration: Episode A: carbon/LiCoO2 nonaqueous rechargeable configuration in Yoshino’s development account. Episode B: representative high-energy cylindrical 18650 cells, not every chemistry.
episode.task: Store rechargeable energy in small/light packages for portable devices; lower manufacturing cost per energy capacity while meeting application requirements.
episode.population: One corporate research pathway; separate reconstructed representative cell datasets assembled from publications/reports.
contemporary_alternatives: Rejected metallic-lithium/PA rechargeable designs in the studied pathway
episode.adoption_measure: Commercialization date and qualitative use; modelled cost per Wh of representative cells, not a complete production or user adoption census.
episode.observation_limits: Retrospective inventor report; sparse early components/process data; choice of high-energy 18650 excludes applications optimized for other characteristics.

actors.chooser: Corporate research and manufacturing teams, device designers and end purchasers with different constraints.
actors.payer: Company research/manufacturing investment and downstream device buyers; public research contributions acknowledged but exact incidence not reconstructed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Materials researchers, process/quality engineers and factory workers; testing drew on another corporate division’s facilities.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Workers and communities involved in materials supply and disposal; mining/waste distribution not investigated by these two sources.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Research teams could reject material routes; consumers faced device offerings. Worker and supply-community refusal evidence unknown.

labour.tasks: Electrode/material development, cell assembly and formation, inspection, manufacturing-process optimization and qualification testing.
labour.entry_barriers: Materials knowledge, controlled processes, equipment and quality/safety capability; exact skill credentials and employment access not established.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Corporate patents/assets and proprietary process formulations matter; ownership of gains and worker bargaining not measured.
labour.transition: No longitudinal labour or mining-community evidence; dates describe technology work, not individual retraining duration.
labour.distribution: Modeled labour/overhead costs aggregated; no supported distribution of compensation, health risk or returns.
labour.evidence_limit: A small assigned learning-by-doing share is not an estimate of factory labour’s value; battery-cost decline is not a worker welfare estimate.

title: Chinese electric two-wheelers: lead-acid persistence and shifted externalities
region: China; sampled urban markets and regional electricity systems
summary: Lead-acid storage supported a growing electric vehicle category while newer batteries remained costly alternatives. City rules, modular component supply, actual substituted modes and upstream lead flows complicate a clean/newer-is-better story.

stages.invention: Lead-acid chemistry predates the episode; the innovation here is a configured vehicle/supply system.
stages.feasibility: Standardized batteries, motors, controllers and chargers assembled into useful low-speed vehicles.
stages.deployment: Observed use and sales expansion in Chinese cities during the 2000s.
stages.diffusion: Industry sales estimates and limited city surveys; no nationally representative household diffusion panel.
stages.scaling: Decentralized supplier/assembler networks; routine assembly observed at six plants.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Li-ion/NiMH available but limited in domestic stores; lead-acid continued. Some cities restricted e-bikes.
stages.displacement/reversal: Prior bicycle/bus use common in surveyed cities; not evidence of universally replacing cars or motorcycles.

counterevidence: Battery choice motives not causally observed; advanced-battery production includes exports; environmental inventory omits important pathways and dose-response evidence.

episode.technology_configuration: Chinese bicycle-style and scooter-style electric two-wheelers, mostly VRLA batteries, with Li-ion/NiMH comparators.
episode.task: Affordable urban/regional personal mobility under local road rules; assemble/maintain a saleable vehicle.
episode.population: Users, dealers and manufacturers in selected cities/plants; national industry estimates and a separate partial emissions model.
episode.interval: 1999–2009, field observations principally 2006–2007; some upstream lead inputs refer to 1999.
contemporary_alternatives: Cars for households able to afford them
Li-ion/NiMH electric two-wheelers, available but more costly
episode.adoption_measure: Industry annual-sales estimates, city roadside shares, prior-mode surveys; chemical-market shares do not cleanly distinguish exports from domestic use.
episode.observation_limits: Nonrandom cities/plants, shifting regulations and inconsistent estimates; emissions model uses borrowed factors and scenario service life/load assumptions.

actors.chooser: Users selecting among affordable/legal modes; city authorities setting access; assemblers selecting components.
actors.payer: Purchasers and replacement-battery buyers; external pollution costs partly borne elsewhere and unpriced in purchase comparison.
actors.operator_maintainer: Riders/households charge vehicles, dealers/repairers replace components, assembly workers build vehicles and battery workers/recyclers handle materials.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Pedestrians, road users, workers and communities near electricity generation, lead production and recycling.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Motorcycle/e-bike bans remove particular options in different cities; surveyed users retained bicycle/bus alternatives but access varied. Communities exposed to upstream pollution did not choose each vehicle; effective refusal rights unestablished.

labour.tasks: Prefabricated-component assembly using pneumatic tools, battery manufacture/replacement, charging and recycling; low machining requirement in visited assembly plants.
labour.entry_barriers: Modular components lowered some assembler technical requirements; capital, supplier access, legal registration and quality control remained. User purchase price and local legal access constrain uptake.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Many small assemblers and competitive supplier networks documented; wages, ownership profits and recycler bargaining not established.
labour.transition: No tracked transitions from bicycle manufacture or displaced transport jobs; plant visits provide task snapshots.
labour.distribution: Pollution shifted to supply/recycling locations; actual worker doses, health outcomes and income distribution not measured.
labour.evidence_limit: Low task-entry requirements are not proof of decent work, and cheap transport is not sufficient evidence of net social benefit.
